entry: Mexican-American actor and civil rights activist. Born in Chihuahua, Mexico, and raised in [[El Paso, Texas]] and East Los Angeles, he played more than 100 film, television and stage roles over his career. He won two [[Academy Awards]], for Best Supporting Actor in *Viva Zapata!* (1952), becoming the first Mexican-born performer to win an Academy Award, and in 1957 for *Lust for Life*. He also painted and wrote several autobiographical books.

Infectious disease caused by the bacterium *Bacillus anthracis*. Infection typically occurs through contact with the skin, inhalation or intestinal absorption of spores, which often appear in infected animal products, and symptoms appear between one day and two months after exposure. Skin infections represent more than 95% of cases; without treatment the risk of death from skin anthrax is 23.7%. Human anthrax is most common in Africa and central and southern Asia, with at least 2,000 cases a year worldwide. A [[Vaccine|vaccine]] is recommended for people at high risk, and two months of [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]] after exposure can prevent infection. Anthrax has been used as a biological weapon since 1916, notably by the Empire of Japan's [[Unit 731]] against China in [[World War II]].

Proposition in [[Cosmology|cosmology]] and philosophy of science that the range of possible observations of the [[Universe|universe]] is limited, because observations can be made only in a universe capable of producing observers. Proponents argue that it explains why the universe has the age and fundamental physical constants needed for intelligent life. Philosopher Nick Bostrom counts thirty formulations, usually divided into weak and strong forms. Critics of the weak form argue that its lack of falsifiability makes it non-scientific, and all versions have been accused of discouraging the search for a deeper physical explanation.

Proposed geologic epoch following the [[Holocene]], during which humanity has become a planetary force of change. Eugene F. Stoermer is credited with coining the term informally in the 1980s, and Paul J. Crutzen popularized it. In 2024 the International Commission on Stratigraphy and the International Union of Geological Sciences rejected the proposal to make it a formal unit of the geologic time scale, but the term remains in use among Earth scientists, social scientists, politicians and the public.

Attribution of human personality, appearance, conduct, cognition or other attributes to non-human entities, often including animals. In fiction and folklore it means endowing non-human characters with human-like behavior, speech and facial expressions, as in talking animals and sentient toys. The tendency is considered innate to human psychology, and most cultures have traditional [[Fable|fables]] with anthropomorphized animals. The term was first attested in 1753, originally in reference to applying a human form to the Christian God. Personification, a related literary device, attributes human form or traits to objects, nations, emotions and natural forces.

Genus of about 1,000 species of flowering plants, the largest genus in the arum family, Araceae. The plants are native to the Americas, from northern Mexico to northern Argentina and parts of the Caribbean. Most are herbs that grow as epiphytes on other plants, and their spathes, which are often brightly colored, are the main focus of breeders. Anthurium andraeanum and A. scherzerianum are the only common cultivated species with bright red spathes. All parts of the plants contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic to cats, dogs and horses. Many hybrids are grown as houseplants, and most commercial propagation is by tissue culture.

Measures designed to nullify or reduce the effectiveness of hostile air action, also called air defense. It encompasses surface-based, submarine-launched and air-based weapons, together with sensor systems, command and control arrangements and passive measures such as barrage balloons. Its origins lie in [[World War I]], when existing artillery was adapted to target reconnaissance aircraft and balloons. Until the 1950s, guns firing ballistic munitions from 7.62 mm to 152.4 mm (6 in) were the standard weapons; guided missiles then became dominant, except at the shortest ranges. During [[World War II]], [[Radar|radar]]-directed fire control and the proximity fuze improved effectiveness. Modern systems are optimized for short-, medium- or long-range defense, and layered air defense combines several tiers so that an attacking aircraft must penetrate all of them. Missiles used include the [[Surface-to-air missile|surface-to-air missiles]] that are now the main weapon of air defense.

Opposition to religious authority in social and political matters, especially the influence of the clergy. In Christian traditions it has historically opposed the influence of Catholicism. During the [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]], some opposed clergy over moral corruption, institutional problems or differences in interpretation, and others opposed their political and economic privileges. It became extremely violent during the [[French Revolution]]. The Civil Constitution of the Clergy, passed on July 12, 1790, required clerics to swear allegiance to the government, and all but seven of the 160 bishops refused. During the [[Reign of Terror]], 30,000 priests were exiled and hundreds more were killed. [[Maximilien Robespierre|Robespierre]] and the Committee of Public Safety later denounced the dechristianization campaign. Under [[Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte]] the [[Catholic Church]] was re-established in France by the Concordat of 1801. Proponents justified anti-clerical measures as responses to clerical alliances with oppressive regimes; critics argued that anti-clerical fervor sometimes devolved into indiscriminate attacks on religious practice.

Optical coating applied to lenses, other optical elements and [[Solar cell|solar cells]] to reduce reflection. Many coatings are transparent thin films with alternating layers of contrasting [[Refractive index|refractive indices]], with thicknesses chosen so that reflected beams interfere destructively. In [[Camera|cameras]], [[Binoculars|binoculars]], [[Telescope|telescopes]] and microscopes the coating improves contrast by eliminating stray light, which is especially important in planetary astronomy. On eyeglass lenses the benefit is mainly cosmetic, though it also lets slightly more light through. The simplest form was discovered by Lord Rayleigh in 1886, when he found that old, tarnished glass transmitted more light than new glass. A bare glass-air interface reflects 4–5% of visible light per surface, and effective coatings can reduce this to below 1%.

Large [[Protein|protein]], also called an immunoglobulin, used by the [[Immune system|immune system]] to identify and neutralize antigens such as those on [[Bacteria|bacteria]] and viruses. Each antibody recognizes one or more specific antigens. The paratope at the tip of each branch of the Y-shaped molecule binds a particular epitope, allowing antibodies to tag an antigen for attack by immune cells or to neutralize it directly, for example by blocking a part of a [[Virus|virus]] needed to invade a host cell. Antibodies may be borne on the surface of a B cell or secreted freely, and the term antibody usually refers to the secreted form. In humans there are five classes: IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and IgM, which differ in their effector functions and where they are released in the body. Antibodies are generally considered part of the adaptive immune system, and they are a manifestation of immunological memory.

Figure in Christian eschatology, prophesied to oppose Christ and falsely substitute himself as savior before the [[Second Coming]]. The term appears four times in the [[New Testament]], all in the Johannine epistles, where interpretations differ: it may denote a category of deceivers rather than a single individual, while later Christian tradition developed a singular end-times figure. Early Church Fathers such as [[Irenaeus]] linked the figure to the Roman Empire. During the [[Reformation]], many Protestant leaders identified the [[Pope|papacy]] as the Antichrist, a view held by [[Martin Luther]] and [[John Calvin]]. Catholic, Orthodox and other traditions generally see the Antichrist as a future deceiver.

Macedonian general and successor of [[Alexander the Great]], founder of the Antigonid dynasty (r. 306–301 BC). The name Monophthalmus means the One-Eyed, and a story recorded by Plutarch says he lost an eye at the siege of Perinthus in 340 BC. He likely served under [[Philip II of Macedon]] and was appointed satrap of [[Phrygia]] by Alexander. After Alexander's death in 323 BC he received Pamphylia and Lycia, but he was driven from Phrygia by the regent Perdiccas and allied with Antipater. In 306 BC he assumed the title of king. For a time he was the most powerful of Alexander's successors, controlling Greece, Asia Minor, Syria and [[Phoenicia]], until a coalition of Cassander, Seleucus, Ptolemy and Lysimachus defeated and killed him at the Battle of Ipsus. His son Demetrius seized [[Macedonia (ancient kingdom)|Macedonia]] in 294 BC. The Antigonid dynasty ruled Macedonia until its conquest by the [[Roman Republic]] in 168 BC.

Country in the [[Lesser Antilles]], comprising [[Antigua]], Barbuda and dozens of smaller islands (pop., 2024: 102,634). Its total area is 440 sq km (170 sq mi), and the country is mostly flat. Most of the population lives on Antigua, and the most populous city is St. John's. The country became independent from Britain on November 1, 1981, and is a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] with [[Charles III]] as head of state. It is a [[Unitary state|unitary state]] in which Barbuda has been administered by the Barbuda Council since 1976. The Labour Party has dominated national politics since 2014. Antigua and Barbuda is a high-income country and the most developed in the Caribbean by the [[Human Development Index]]. Tourism generates nearly 60% of GDP.

Ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, the oldest known analog computer. It could predict astronomical positions and [[Eclipse|eclipses]] decades in advance and track the four-year cycle of the [[Ancient Olympic Games]]. Its fragments were recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera and are held by the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Estimates of its construction date range from about 87 BC to 205 BC, and the shipwreck is dated to approximately 70–60 BC. Its surviving bronze gears imply that the mechanism modeled the motion of the Moon, including its irregular speed, a motion studied by the astronomer [[Hipparchus]], who may have been consulted in its construction.

Hostility, prejudice or discrimination against Jews. Racial antisemitism holds that Jews form a distinct race with inferior traits, while religious antisemitism stems from hostility to Judaism, often through doctrines of supersession found in other [[Abrahamic religions]]. The compound word *Antisemitismus* was first used in print in Germany in 1879 as a scientific-sounding term for *Judenhass*, meaning Jew-hatred. Most of the world's violent antisemitic events have occurred in Europe, where modern antisemitism emerged from Christian hostility during the [[Middle Ages]]. Racial theories of the 19th and 20th centuries peaked in the Nazi [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]], which murdered six million Jews. Debate continues over whether anti-Zionism or criticism of [[Israel]] can constitute antisemitism.

[[Personality disorder]] characterized by a chronic pattern of behavior that disregards the rights and well-being of others. It usually manifests in childhood or early adolescence, before age 15, and symptoms tend to peak in late adolescence and early adulthood. People with severe symptoms have higher rates of divorce, unemployment, homelessness and incarceration, and an elevated risk of [[Suicide|suicide]]. Symptoms may diminish after age 40, though only a small percentage of people improve significantly. No medication is approved specifically for the disorder.

French painter and draughtsman credited with inventing the genre of *fêtes galantes*, scenes of bucolic and idyllic charm with a theatrical air. His brief career revived interest in color and movement in the tradition of [[Peter Paul Rubens|Rubens]] and Correggio, and he shifted the waning [[Baroque]] style toward the less formal, more naturalistic [[Rococo]]. He moved to Paris in 1702 and absorbed the characters of the [[Commedia dell'arte]], which became a lifelong subject. Many of his works feature figures from Italian comedy and ballet in idyllic outdoor settings. In 1709 he placed second in the Prix de Rome, and in 1717 he gained full membership of the Académie royale with *Pilgrimage to the Isle of Cythera*, now in the [[Louvre]]. He died of [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]].

Austrian composer and organist best known for his symphonies and sacred music, including Masses, a Te Deum and motets. His symphonies, with their rich harmonic language, strongly polyphonic character and considerable length, are considered emblematic of the final stage of Austro-German [[Romanticism]]. Bruckner was critical of his own work and often revised his compositions, so many works exist in several versions, and scholars continue to debate which versions reflect his intentions. Detractors, including the critic Eduard Hanslick and supporters of [[Johannes Brahms]], pointed to the symphonies' large size and use of repetition. The composer [[Gustav Mahler]], a friend, greatly admired him. He moved to [[Vienna]] in 1868.

Russian playwright, short-story writer and physician. He began writing stories to earn money, but his formal innovations influenced the development of the modern short story. Along with [[Henrik Ibsen|Ibsen]] and [[August Strindberg|Strindberg]], he is regarded as one of the three seminal figures in the birth of early [[Modernism|modernism]] in the theater. His four major plays, *The Seagull*, *Uncle Vanya*, *Three Sisters* and *The Cherry Orchard*, replace conventional action with a theater of mood. *The Seagull* was revived in 1898 by [[Konstantin Stanislavski]]'s Moscow Art Theatre. Chekhov practiced medicine throughout his career, calling it his lawful wife and literature his mistress. In 1890 he traveled to [[Sakhalin]], and his factual account *The Island of Sakhalin* (1893–1895) helped prompt penal reforms.

Sixth king of the [[Seleucid Empire]] (r. 223–187 BC). He succeeded his brother Seleucus III Ceraunus, who was murdered in Anatolia, and inherited a state in turmoil. His initial campaign against [[Ptolemaic Kingdom|Ptolemaic Egypt]] failed, but over the following decade he reasserted Seleucid authority in central Asia Minor, Parthia and [[Bactria]], pressing as far as the Kabul valley and earning the epithet the Great. He then brought Coele-Syria, [[Phoenicia]] and Judea under Seleucid control. Declaring himself the champion of Greek freedom against Roman domination, he fought Rome from 192 BC, advised by [[Hannibal]], and was defeated at Thermopylae (191 BC) and Magnesia (190 BC), losing much of the Seleucid land in Asia Minor. He died on an expedition to the east.

Particle corresponding to each type of ordinary particle, with the same mass but opposite charges. The antiparticle of the electron is the [[Positron|positron]], while some particles, such as the [[Photon|photon]], are their own antiparticle. A particle and its antiparticle annihilate each other, producing photons. Because charge is conserved, antiparticles are produced by natural processes such as beta decay and cosmic-ray collisions, or by pair production in accelerators such as the [[Large Hadron Collider]] at [[CERN]]. The laws of nature are nearly symmetrical between particles and antiparticles, but the discovery of charge parity violation showed that this symmetry is only approximate, and the question of why matter dominates the universe remains unanswered. Carl D. Anderson discovered the positron in 1932 in cosmic-ray tracks, and Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain found the antiproton in 1955 at the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California, Berkeley]].

Matter composed of [[Antiparticle|antiparticles]], which have the same mass as their ordinary partners but opposite electric charge. When a particle meets its antiparticle the two annihilate, producing intense gamma rays, neutrinos and other particles, with energy proportional to the total mass involved in accordance with E=mc². Antimatter occurs naturally in [[Cosmic ray|cosmic ray]] collisions and some radioactive decays, and it is essential to applications such as positron emission tomography, [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]] and industrial imaging. Antiparticles can form antiatoms, but only a small total amount has been artificially produced, and no macroscopic amount has ever been assembled. The observable [[Universe|universe]] appears composed almost entirely of ordinary matter, an asymmetry that remains one of the great unsolved problems in physics.

Chemical element (symbol Sb, atomic number 51), a lustrous grey [[Metalloid|metalloid]] that occurs mainly as the sulfide mineral stibnite (Sb₂S₃). Antimony compounds have been known since ancient history, when they were powdered for use as cosmetics, known as *kohl*, and as medicine. China is the largest producer, with most output coming from the Xikuangshan Mine in Hunan. Its most common use is in alloys with [[Lead|lead]] and [[Tin|tin]] for solders, bullets and plain bearings, and it improves the rigidity of lead-acid battery plates. Antimony trioxide is a prominent additive in halogen-containing flame retardants, and antimony is used as a dopant in [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] devices. Its toxicity is comparable to that of [[Arsenic|arsenic]]. The element makes up about 0.2 parts per million of the Earth's crust.

Hellenistic city founded in 300 BC on the Orontes River, at the site of modern Antakya, Turkey. It was founded by [[Seleucus I Nicator]], a successor of [[Alexander the Great]], and it became the capital of the [[Seleucid Empire]] from 240 BC until 63 BC, when the Romans took control. It was then the capital of Roman Syria, and at its peak it may have had more than 500,000 inhabitants, making it the third largest city in the [[Roman Empire]] after Rome and Alexandria. It was a center of Hellenistic Judaism and one of the cities of the pentarchy, and it is called the cradle of Christianity; the [[New Testament]] asserts that the name Christian first emerged there. The city declined in the [[Middle Ages]] because of warfare, repeated earthquakes and changing trade routes.

Island in the [[Lesser Antilles]], the most populous island of [[Antigua and Barbuda]] (pop., 2011: 83,191). Its area is 281 sq km (108 sq mi) and its perimeter roughly 87 km. [[Christopher Columbus]] was the first European to visit it, in 1493, and British colonization began in 1632. The main city, St. John's, has more than 22,000 people and a deep harbor able to accommodate large cruise ships. The economy relies mainly on tourism, and English Harbour on the southeastern coast is a leading yachting destination.
